title: Saudi Arabia cancels 'Davos in the Desert' due to Yemen's Houthi strikes
description: Britain offers military support as Saudi cancels renowned 'Davos in desert" investor meeting due to strikes from Houthi forces in Yemen.
content:
Britain offers military support as Saudi cancels renowned 'Davos in desert" investor meeting due to strikes from Houthi forces in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia is getting more international support in its war against the Houthis.
Support from the U.K., which is sending fighter jets. Saudi Arabia already has military support from France, Turkey and Pakistan, and the U.S. is sharing intelligence on Houthi targets. So what difference will all that make?
MARTÍNEZ: Joining us now to explain is NPR correspondent in Dubai, Aya Batrawy. So, Aya, what do we know about the mission for these British jets?
AYA BATRAWY, BYLINE: OK. The U.K. hasn't said how many Royal Air Force jets it's sending but says this is a purely defensive mission to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure against Houthi attacks. The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, they have hit Saudi airports, oil and gas sites, military bases and even the offices of Saudi oil giant Aramco.
Now, the U.K. made clear, however, that its air force will not be conducting offensive attacks on the Houthis, though it does have a refueling aircraft assisting Saudi jets in their bombings of the Houthis in Yemen. And, A, there's another country that looks poised to send military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and that is Egypt. It could deploy troops there, drawing a major regional country into this war that until now has been trying to mediate an end to the fighting.
MARTÍNEZ: Why does Saudi Arabia appear to be struggling to defend its infrastructure, things like airports?
BATRAWY: So Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars a year on its defense, but Houthi attacks have pierced through those defenses time and again. Now, I asked Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, why that is. She told me the Houthis in Yemen are using new tactics that Iran also used over this past year of war. Have a listen.
ELIZABETH DENT: I don't know necessarily that this is, like, a capability gap, per se, but just that the tactics have pretty drastically changed, right? Like, we've seen the Iranians employ this tactic as well, where they'll send drone swarms to sort of take out the initial line of defenses. And then we'll have ballistic and cruise missiles come in, and cruise missiles are particularly hard to track because they often fly under radar.
BATRAWY: And an example of this was released last night by the Houthis in a video showing a swarm of armed drones fitted with cameras striking Saudi troops along the Saudi-Yemeni border. The Saudis have not commented on that. But the Houthis also claimed responsibility for missile attacks this week that the Yemeni government says killed more than 50 Yemeni security recruits in central Yemen. This is the deadliest attack in the country in years.
And as this war grinds on, A, and more people are killed, there's real consequences for the Saudi crown prince. Houthi attacks on Saudi airports forced the kingdom to cancel an annual investment forum dubbed Davos in the Desert that was scheduled for next week. Now, this exclusive event had shown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ability over the years to draw the world's top money managers to the Saudi capital as part of his economic overhaul of the country, but those ambitions are now colliding hard with this war.
MARTÍNEZ: Yeah. You mentioned those attacks in Yemen. What are aid agencies saying about the situation in Yemen right now?
BATRAWY: So the U.N. says more than a quarter million people have been displaced in recent weeks. That number continues to rise. The situation is especially concerning in the southwestern city of Taiz. The Houthis have encircled that city, cutting off supplies from the government-run city of Aden, and prices there have skyrocketed for hundreds of thousands of besieged people. And the World Health Organization says hospitals in Taiz have only a few days of fuel left.
MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Aya Batrawy in Dubai. Thank you very much.

title: As the U.S. population ages rapidly, meet the people stepping up to offer care
description: The burden of caring for America's aging population falls on family caregivers. It can take a toll on their lives and mental health.
content:
The burden of caring for America's aging population falls on family caregivers. It can take a toll on their lives and mental health.
America is aging fast. Every day, 10,000 people turn 65, and a majority of them will eventually need long-term care, which Medicare mostly doesn't pay for. It seems like a brewing crisis, but so far, the burden falls on family caregivers. There's been virtually no help from the federal government. Caregiving is almost invisible work that's rarely acknowledged. We're talking to reporter Kat McGowan, a Rosalynn Carter mental health journalism fellow at the Carter Center, who's bringing us a series of portraits of caregivers, giving voice to a community that's often taken for granted. Kat, welcome to the program.
RASCOE: So can you tell us more about family caregivers? What do they do, and what work do they take on?
MCGOWAN: They do everything from helping their loved one shower and dress to supervising home dialysis. There are about 63 million family caregivers in the United States, and if they were paid for their time, the bill would add up to about $600 billion a year, which, for context, is more than all out-of-pocket spending on health care for everyone in the country.
RASCOE: Wow. So are there any policies in the works to help support caregivers?
MCGOWAN: There's not much on the federal level, even though the idea has strong bipartisan support. Some of the states have created small tax credits for caregivers or changed workplace leave laws to help, but caregivers are mostly on their own to handle the huge responsibility.
RASCOE: That sounds like it would really take a toll on your mental health. You've talked to a lot of people in this situation. How is it affecting them?
MCGOWAN: Many family caregivers are stressed out and lonely, with high rates of depression and anxiety. Yet caregiving can be profoundly meaningful despite its difficulties. One person I talked to was Karla Rodriguez (ph), a 41-year-old who works in human resources in Denver. She cares for her father, who has diabetes, HIV and alcoholism, among other problems. Rodriguez is one of the so-called sandwich caregivers, balancing his needs with work and parenting. Here's what she told me.
KARLA RODRIGUEZ: As a caregiver for my father, I'm on call, where if he's refusing to go to dialysis one day, or there's an issue with a bill, or he needs to go get something, no matter if it's his HIV meds or diet coke, like, I'm on call. And there's something about that low-grade stress of not knowing, or maybe even worse, knowing that something is going to happen, you just don't know when, that really wears on you.
MCGOWAN: On top of the stress, like a lot of caregivers, she deals with guilt.
RODRIGUEZ: This is all pulling away time with my own children and my work. None of it stops. It's all still there. And I think that's something that caregivers constantly struggle with, which is, am I giving enough of myself to everyone who needs the care?
MCGOWAN: The thing is, Rodriguez and her dad weren't always close. Her dad had drifted in and out of her life and let her down more times than she can count. Eventually, the alcoholism and other diseases caught up with him. His life really fell apart, and she had to make a decision.
RODRIGUEZ: I will never forget, it was November 2023. I get a call from a hospital to go see him in the emergency room. And I went there, and I'm sitting there for a while, and then I realized they actually had put me next to my father, and I hadn't even recognized him. He also had not recognized me. That was a very hard moment. We both were confronted with the cold, hard facts of the situation we were in.
MCGOWAN: Given the circumstances, many people would've walked away. I asked her why she didn't.
RODRIGUEZ: I think I knew that I was the end of the line. If I hadn't stepped up, he would be dead, and he would've been dead quickly. And I just could not, in good conscience, have that on my hands.
MCGOWAN: Her father's been sober for two years now. Rodriguez understands her father better now and forgives him. And that's the thing about caregiving - it can be brutal, but there can also be unexpected rewards.
RODRIGUEZ: I've gotten to know more about my dad, more about his background, more about his own trauma. And so I have a lot of empathy for him and what got him into the situation that he was in. Yeah, oddly enough, I would say our relationship is better now than it's been in years. And I never thought that my children would have a memory of him, and they actually look forward to seeing him now.
MCGOWAN: She and her dad are open and honest with each other for the first time.
RODRIGUEZ: There's a level of transparency in our relationship that we've never had before, ever. And I know all of his scars and skeletons in his closet for the most part, and he gets to see that I love him regardless of that.
MCGOWAN: So you can hear how resourceful and strong caregivers can be, and they have to be. Like Rodriguez, most people are doing this on their own without much financial or practical support.
RASCOE: Reporter Kat McGowan. Thank you so much.

title: How people are finding community through the tile game Mahjong
description: More people around the U.S. are picking up the centuries-old tile game Mahjong and uncovering new community connections in the process.
content:
Attendees learn and play American Mahjong at the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington, D.C. In-person meetups to play Mahjong are growing in popularity along with interest in the game. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
A surge of interest in the Chinese tile game Mahjong is building a community in Washington, D.C., as players of all ages look for joy, in-person connection and time off of their phones.
First introduced in the U.S . in the 1920s, the centuries-old game consists of tiles that players must place in specific combinations. Both physical and digital versions of the game have remained of interest worldwide. But over the last year, the game has seen increased interest specifically among Gen Z and Millennials — including through social media content focused on the gameplay and history of Mahjong.
In-person meetups to play Mahjong are also growing in popularity, and NPR had the opportunity to visit the Capital Jewish Museum on a Sunday afternoon in D.C. for a free drop-in game of Mahjong. The gathering featured two tables overflowing with folks that were there to learn the game for the first time, while others with a wide range of experiences played at tables around them.
You can listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue play button above. And you can view a selection of images from the drop-in Mahjong event below.
One of the event's organizers, David Horowitz (center), teaches a class to new students. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
Claire Boyle (left) and Katie Murray (right) learn to play American Mahjong. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
Attendees look over the rules at the Mahjong drop-in event. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
Grace Folk (left), Sophia Rosso, Andrew Maisel, and Will Tucker-Ray learn to play American Mahjong. Roommates Folk and Rosso said that they are trying new, inexpensive hobbies that get them out of the house and off their phones. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
Event co-organizer Jon Gann teaches new students. He is proud that he and Horowitz have built a grassroots community around Mahjong. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
Typically, the game is played with four people at a square table but some folks are doubled up with their friends. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption
"We're in an age right now where people are looking for joy, and this gives people a good time for a few hours," David Horowitz said. Maansi Srivastava for NPR hide caption

title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
description: Sitting at a desk all day hurts. And it isn't good for us. Strategies to make it a little more comfortable, from eye muscle exercises to alleviate eye strain to a back pain-fighting body movement.
content:
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters . Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.
For more ergonomic tips, read our story .
This story includes reporting from Ruth Tam, Sylvie Douglis, Frank Festa, Andee Tagle, Manoush Zomorodi and Margaret Cirino. This story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
description: President Trump's attempts to bring beef prices down has potentially backfired politically in several key states.
content:
Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas, on September 11, 2026. RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images hide caption
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.
"They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.
When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."
Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.
All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.
"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.
It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.
"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."
Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..
Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases . In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.
And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.
That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.
"If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."
This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.
From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption .
That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.
All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.
"We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News . "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."
Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.
"She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."
In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.
Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.
"Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."
Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.
"I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.
Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.
"As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.
He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.
"They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."
This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year – Texas, Nebraska, Montana, and Kansas – are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.
Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."
Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a non partisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.
As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.
"I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."
Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.

title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
description: President Trump, seeking to reshape the voting map, prompted a rare wave of mid-decade redistricting that gave Republicans a boost for holding the House. But the voters will determine if it works.
content:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214 .
In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)
But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.
Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.
Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.
Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.
In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities .
In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s , when courts set the current rules.
Here's where states redistricted - or didn't.

title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
description: A drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become a focus for American companies searching for locations to place their data centers.
content:
ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.
This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.
Heavy equipment excavates an area adjacent to an Amazon data center currently under construction in Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. Local authorities have approved dozens of data center projects for U.S. Big Tech and other companies that will transform the character of this region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.
"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."
An Amazon data center, currently under construction, is seen in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Aragon authorities say they are betting that hosting data centers will place them at the center of a "new economy" they believe AI will bring. But many local residents and activist groups believe these projects are delivering an environmental crisis. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
An Amazon data center, currently under construction beside the quiet village of Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. It's being built beside the village on land close to a protected wetland. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Companies building data centers in Spain's Aragon region say they will mostly rely on renewable energy. But the centers will also sometimes be powered by on-site generators. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)
The Sotonera reservoir, which serves population centers and farms in the provinces of Huesca and Zaragoza, is seen in Tormos, Spain, on Sept. 29. This is one of Spain's driest regions that, with climate change, is already suffering from repeated drought. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.
Farmland that is to be developed into a data center complex is seen in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents of Botorrita village say they first learned of the project when they found the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. The government of Aragon is fast-tracking planning permissions under a procedure that also significantly cuts the time the public has to object. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.
Residents point to an area that is to be developed into a data center complex in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents say the planned complex comes to within 80 meters of the garden wall of a family living at the village edge. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."
Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.
Julio Enfedaque stands at the edge of a construction site where an outflow pipe will be installed that he says will carry water from a nearby Amazon data center in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Farmers in the region are concerned about the water these data complexes require. In this region already affected by frequent droughts, they fear they will be in competition for the resources to grow their crops. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.
Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.
Julio Enfedaque carries some alfalfa in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. He fears the construction of so many water-hungry data centers in this region will leave him without enough of the resource to grow his crops. His family has farmed here for generations. He believes this way of life is so under threat that he says he is advising his nephews to find other careers. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.
But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.
Swallows fly in front of wind turbines near Huesca, Spain, on Sept. 29. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.
While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.
The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.
Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks at a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, solar panel farms and wind turbines, which has alarmed many local residents with the high energy use, noise pollution, danger to wildlife and heat generation they are known for. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks for raptors and vultures, flying near dozens of windmills, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.
Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.
"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.
Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.
Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.
Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.
Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

title: Bukele says military operation launched to rescue Salvadorans held by gangs in Haiti
description: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti.
content:
Armored police vehicles that are part of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) patrol the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Odelyn Joseph/AP hide caption
SAN SALVADOR — El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti, warning of a more forceful response if they are not released alive and unharmed.
Gangs in Haiti had opened fire on an armored vehicle three days earlier the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country. The four Salvadoran soldiers have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.
Addressing Haitian gang leaders, Bukele demanded that they return the Salvadorans "alive, unharmed" and warned that, if they do so, "everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping." If not, the Salvadoran leader — who drew international attention for his contentious war on his own country's gangs — said it would result in a more powerful operation.
"Today's attack is nothing compared to what is coming if they do not release the four hostages alive. And do not take our words as empty threats," he wrote on the social media platform X.
It was not immediately clear if Bukele intended any further action to be carried out by Salvadoran, Haitian or international security forces in the area.
In his post, the Salvadoran leader shared video of armored vehicles with shattered windows driving through plumes of smoke.
Haiti's government issued a news release Wednesday evening saying the "abduction" of the aviation technicians was an "absolute priority."
It noted that a meeting was held at the prime minister's office "to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force."
"The release of the abducted soldiers is an absolute priority, and all necessary resources are being mobilized to achieve this goal," the government said.
It wasn't immediately clear if Haitian authorities received confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.
A spokesperson for the gang suppression force did not immediately respond to a message seeking details.
Bukele said the four men are aviation technicians and that the Salvadoran mission in Haiti "consists only of pilots and technical personnel" whose main job is to carry out medical evacuations, "not to wage war."
The U.N.-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday's attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops and it comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador is among a number of countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form a part of a gang suppression force with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.
The U.N. in 2025 originally approved up to 5,550 security personnel and more than 50 civilian staff to be sent to Haiti to dismantle armed gangs.
In early October, El Salvador passed a law extending its armed forces' participation in the force for a year. The law also authorized the mission to "deploy civilian and military personnel according to the mission's needs," expanding its role beyond medical evacuations, as stipulated in the previous decree.
The multinational force received at least a six-month extension through March 2027 from the U.N. Security Council.
Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January through mid-September and more than 230 people kidnapped, according to the United Nations.
The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the U.N. and the U.S.

title: Marco Rubio tells senators Venezuela transition won't be fast or easy
description: At his first Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing since U.S. forces seized Nicolás Maduro, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns the U.S. could still use force to pressure Venezuela's government.
content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio appears before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee to explain President Trump's policy toward Venezuela following the U.S. military operation that ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro, at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., Wednesday. J. Scott Applewhite/AP hide caption
Secretary of State Marco Rubio faced intense scrutiny in a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on Wednesday over the Trump administration's military operation that ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, as lawmakers pressed for clarity on what comes next for the South American country and for U.S. involvement in the region.
In his opening remarks, Rubio rejected claims that the United States is at war with Venezuela, insisting the operation was a limited law-enforcement mission rather than a military occupation.
"There is no war against Venezuela, and we did not occupy a country. There are no U.S. troops on the ground," Rubio said, framing the mission as a targeted law enforcement action rather than a military occupation.
Republicans on the committee largely praised the administration's actions. Committee Chairman Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, called the mission an "incredibly brief, targeted and successful raid," noting it resulted in no American casualties.
But Democrats sharply criticized the cost and consequences of the operation. Ranking committee member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., questioned whether removing Maduro was worth the financial and political fallout, citing estimates that the raid and U.S. naval blockade could cost taxpayers up to $1 billion.
"The U.S. naval blockade around Venezuela and the raid have already cost American taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars," Shaheen said. "And yet the Maduro regime is essentially still in power — all the same people are running the country."
Shaheen and other Democrats also raised concerns about Venezuela's interim leader, former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez, arguing she has taken no meaningful steps to reduce Iranian, Chinese or Russian influence in the country. Some senators accused the administration of replacing one authoritarian figure with another.
"The [Drug Enforcement Administration] has reportedly identified Delcy Rodríguez as a significant actor in the drug trade," Shaheen pressed.
Rubio responded that Rodríguez has not been indicted like Maduro and said Washington's immediate priority is stability — even if it requires working with leaders the U.S. does not fully trust.
"We are dealing with individuals that in our system would not be acceptable in the long term," Rubio acknowledged. "But we are in a transition to stabilization phase. You have to work with the people currently in charge of the elements of government."
Lawmakers also questioned financial arrangements tied to Venezuela's oil sector, including reports that the U.S. granted no-bid licenses to two companies — one reportedly tied to a major Trump donor — to sell Venezuelan oil. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said the optics "reek" to many Americans.
Rubio defended the move as a temporary measure, arguing Venezuela was running out of oil storage capacity.
"We had to move that oil very quickly," he said. "The long-term plan is not those two trading companies. The long-term plan is for Venezuela to have a normal energy program that sells directly into the market."
The secretary of state also defended the ongoing U.S. naval blockade, describing it as a "quarantine" rather than a military escalation. He said Venezuela's current leaders are cooperating with U.S. authorities by helping identify ships suspected of sanctions violations.
While most Republicans backed the administration's strategy, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., raised concerns about the legality of the operation and the precedent it sets. Rubio maintained the raid was lawful and necessary to disrupt what he called a "criminal state."
Rubio warned that U.S. patience is not unlimited, signaling a willingness to escalate if cooperation breaks down.
"Make no mistake," he said. "We are prepared to use force to ensure maximum cooperation if other methods fail."
Throughout the hearing, senators repeatedly pressed Rubio on how success would be measured and how — or when — Venezuela would transition to democracy.
"This is not a frozen dinner," Rubio told the committee. "You don't put it in a microwave and 2 1/2 minutes later it's ready. These are complex things."
The hearing marks Rubio's highest-profile test so far on Venezuela policy, as lawmakers from both parties demand clearer benchmarks, greater transparency, and a defined long-term strategy for U.S. involvement in the country.

title: Trump vows to 'take care of Cuba,' praises Venezuela cooperation at summit
description: Trump made the promise in front of an assembled meeting of Latin American leaders.
content:
President Trump signs a proclamation committing to countering cartel criminal activity at the Shield of the Americas Summit. Rebecca Blackwell/AP hide caption
President Trump on Saturday launched the Shield of the Americas Summit – a coalition of Latin American leaders – with a pledge to "take care of Cuba," as the United States increases its intervention in the region.
"Many of you have come today and they say, 'I hope you can take care of Cuba.' Because you have problems with Cuba, right?," Trump said to the gathering of Latin American leadership.
"I was surprised, but four of you said, actually, 'Could you do us a favor?' Take care of Cuba.' I'll take care of it, ok?" he continued to applause from the crowd.
Attending the meeting were the leaders of Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, and Trinidad and Tobago. The event was hosted at the Trump National Doral Miami golf course in Doral, Florida.
His comments follow tension between Cuba and U.S. and as many Cuban-Americans are hoping for a change in regime for the communist nation.
The Trump administration has eased a blockade of Venezuelan oil, allowing some private sector oil sales to Cuba. The country has been experiencing fuel shortages and blackouts that have left millions without power, according to The Associated Press .
Since the United States' capture and arrest of Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro, in January, those who wish to see Cuba's government toppled see Trump's stance on foreign intervention as a signal that America might similarly help orchestrate the ouster of Cuba's Miguel Díaz-Canel.
Speaking to the change in Venezuela's leadership since Maduro's capture, Trump praised acting-President Delcy Rodríguez for her cooperation with the United States.
"She's doing a great job because she's working with us. If she wasn't working with us, I would not say she's doing a great job. In fact, she wasn't working with us, I'd say she's doing a very poor job, unacceptable, but she's doing a great job," Trump said.
He continued that because of U.S. assistance, Venezuela's economic picture was considerably sunnier because of American oil exports and forthcoming gold and mineral trades.
Trump has hailed the transition from Maduro's leadership is the model for regime changes.

title: U.S. military strikes Iran as Trump says negotiations move forward for deal to end war
description: The U.S. military announced strikes against Iranian positions just hours after President Trump says more countries should normalize ties with Israel in any Iran deal, tempering expectations of peace.
content:
People walk past a mural depicting a U.S. aircraft carrier under missile attack by Iran in downtown Tehran, on May 17. The two countries agreed to a ceasefire but strikes have continued including U.S. military strikes against Iranian targets on Monday. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
President Trump and administration officials are tempering expectations of an imminent agreement to end the war with Iran, while calling for more countries in the Middle East to normalize relations with Israel as part of any deal.
Iranian officials have also signaled disagreements on key issues.
The U.S. military announced it struck Iranian boats and missile launch sites Monday in Southern Iran.
U.S. Central Command Spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said in a statement that Iran's boats were attempting to place mines and the military acted in "self-defense."
"U.S. Central Command continues to defend our forces while using restraint during the ongoing ceasefire," Hawkins said.
The current ceasefire was negotiated to allow Iran and the U.S. to negotiate an end to the U.S.-Israel war in Iran.
Trump, after saying Saturday that the U.S. and Iran had "largely negotiated" a memorandum of understanding that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, backed away from the idea that a final deal is imminent.
"Negotiations with the Islamic Republic of Iran are proceeding nicely!" Trump said in a Monday morning post on his Truth Social platform . "It will only be a Great Deal for all or, no Deal at all — Back to the Battlefront and shooting, but bigger and stronger than ever before — And nobody wants that!"
Speaking in New Delhi, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday, the United States would "give diplomacy every chance to succeed before we explore the alternatives."
Iran, meanwhile, has not officially commented on the proposed agreement. But semi-official news agencies, often used for Iranian leadership messaging, have said that disputes over "one or two" issues were jeopardizing the potential deal.
According to the Associated Press, an Iranian delegation led by parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf traveled to Qatar on Monday for talks. Qalibaf led negotiations with Vice President Vance in Pakistan last month.
On Monday, Tasnim news agency, close to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, accused the U.S. of "obstructionism" over the release of some frozen Iranian funds in exchange for lifting restrictions over transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The news agency also said the agreement being negotiated called on Iran to restore the number of ships transiting through the vital waterway to pre-war levels within 30 days and for the U.S. to completely lift its blockade within the same time.
While restoring commercial traffic through the strait has been a top priority for U.S. allies, Trump on Monday added an apparent demand that any peace deal should require more countries to extend full diplomatic recognition to the state of Israel.
"[I]t should be mandatory that all of these Countries, at a minimum, simultaneously, sign onto the Abraham Accords," Trump wrote on social media .
The Abraham Accords , first signed in 2020 during Trump's first term, normalized relations between Israel, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Kazakhstan , Morocco, and Sudan are also signatories.
Trump now says Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia should agree to establish full diplomatic relations with Israel.
Trump suggested that Iran — a long-time foe of Israel — should also sign onto the agreement, saying it would be "an Honor to have them also be part of this unparalleled World Coalition."
Trump's bid to include Iran is a stark contrast from his military threats in April , when he warned Tehran that a "whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again."
His latest effort to expand the frame of the peace talks drew support from his political allies , including Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.), who extolled the plan as "simply brilliant," in a post on X .
He added: "With Saudi Arabia and others like Pakistan making peace with Israel, the region will know a level of stability never dreamed of before President Trump and will eventually lead to regional integration making the Middle East a powerhouse for economic opportunity and good instead of a powder keg."
But Trump's new demands were also described as an unrealistic distraction by some experts on the region.
"I remain a proponent of the Abraham Accords, and their eventual expansion," said Dan Shapiro, former U.S. ambassador to Israel, writing on X . "That said, tying expansion of the Accords to a deal to end the war with Iran is needlessly complicated and unrealistic."
Trump's bid for a sweeping new diplomatic arrangement in the region comes after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, sparking a war that for the first time spread to U.S. allies in the Gulf including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Iran struck U.S. military bases and energy infrastructure in those countries in retaliation for U.S. and Israeli strikes. A ceasefire was agreed in April. Several thousand Iranians were believed killed in the U.S. and Israeli strikes.
While Trump originally focused on the idea of regime change and the perceived threat of Iran building nuclear weapons, current talks have centered on re-opening the Strait of Hormuz.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks to journalists before boarding his plane at Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi on May 25. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Rubio, on an official visit to India, said the agreement being discussed with Iran was "a pretty solid thing on the table in terms of their ability to open up the strait." He said the U.S. intended to engage in "a very real, significant, time-limited negotiation on the nuclear matter."
"Hopefully, we can pull it off," he added.
Iran's state-backed ISNA news agency quoted a senior Iranian diplomat as saying that Iran has not made any commitment in negotiations on the initial agreement on nuclear issues, including highly enriched uranium.
The U.S. has pressed Iran to send highly enriched uranium out of the country for safe-keeping. Iran, which says its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes, sees it as a sovereignty issue and has indicated opposition to that option.
Hossein Nooshabadi, a senior foreign ministry official quoted by Iran's ISNA news agency, said Iran's demands include "ending the war on all fronts including Lebanon, releasing billions of dollars of Iran's frozen assets, lifting the U.S. naval blockade and opening the Strait of Hormuz, withdrawing U.S. forces from the surrounding environment of the Islamic Republic, and the freedom to sell Iranian oil are envisioned in the potential agreement between Iran and the United States."
Trump wrote Saturday the U.S. would continue its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz until an agreement with Iran was "⁠reached, certified, and signed."
Iran's parliament spokesman Ebrahim Rezaei said in a social media post that Iran would not yield to threats and if the U.S. wanted an agreement it should negotiate but if it wanted even higher prices at the gas pumps it should "continue bluffing".
Israel, which has played a key role in Trump's decision-making on Iran, is strongly opposed to a deal that includes a stop to the war in Lebanon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that, in a call with Trump on Saturday, the president "reaffirmed Israel's right to defend itself against threats on every front, including Lebanon."
Despite a U.S.-brokered extension to the ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon this month, Israel has continued to occupy southern Lebanon and launch waves of airstrikes. Lebanon's health ministry says more than 3,200 people, including women, children, medical personnel and first responders, have been killed in Israeli attacks since the war with the Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah began in March.
Israel says 22 soldiers and a military contractor along with two civilians have been killed in Hezbollah attacks.

title: No Deal: U.S.-Iran peace talks in Islamabad fall through
description: The United States and Iran failed to reach an agreement after a day of highly anticipated face-to-face peace talks, Washington's lead negotiator Vice President J.D. Vance announced on Sunday.
content:
A police officer walks past a billboard regarding the United States and Iran negotiations, outside a media facilitation center in Islamabad, Pakistan, Saturday, April 11, 2026. Anjum Naveed/AP hide caption
ISLAMABAD – The United States and Iran failed to reach an agreement after a day of highly anticipated face-to-face peace talks, Washington's lead negotiator Vice President J.D. Vance announced on Sunday.
"The bad news is that we have not reached an agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the US... they have chosen not to accept our terms," Vance said in a press conference in Islamabad, before boarding Airforce Two to leave the country.
Asked what the major sticking point had been that led to the breakdown in negotiations, Vance said: "The simple fact is that we need to see an affirmative commitment that they will not seek a nuclear weapon, and they will not seek the tools that would enable them to quickly achieve a nuclear weapon."
However, he left open the possibility an agreement could still be reached, saying: "We leave here with a very simple proposal: a method of understanding that is our final and best offer," adding, "We'll see if the Iranians accept it."
The talks — which lasted for 21 hours — began in Islamabad on Saturday as the two sides looked to reach a deal to end the war that has shaken the Middle East for six weeks. It was the first face-to-face engagement between the U.S. and Iran since 2015, when the Obama administration negotiated a nuclear deal with Iran that was later scrapped by Trump.
The negotiations took place amid a fragile ceasefire between the two countries, made even more shaky following Israel's continued strikes on Lebanon and Iran's demand to maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz.
On Saturday, Israel's military said had it struck more than 200 targets in Lebanon affiliated with the Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah in the past 24 hours.
Iran, under its 10-point negotiation plan, demanded an end to Israel's attacks against Hezbollah as part of any permanent agreement. Other demands from the Iranian delegation included the release of $6 billion in frozen assets, guarantees around its nuclear program and the right to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
President Donald Trump's demands, meanwhile, have shifted since the United States and Israel first launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
Vice President JD Vance walks to speak with the Press before boarding Air Force Two, Friday, April 10, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md., for expected departure to Pakistan, for talks on Iran. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption
On Friday, Trump said that the main objective to end the war was to prevent Iran from having any nuclear capabilities.
"No nuclear weapon. That's 99% percent of it," Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One in Maryland.
Trump has also said the goals for the war with Iran included destroying its military capabilities and creating regime change – neither of which have happened.
Saturday's meeting in Islamabad is the culmination of weeks of frantic diplomacy by Pakistan's leaders, who pitched the city as the venue for talks even before they took the lead as a key mediator that both the U.S. and Iran credited for helping broker a two-week ceasefire.
The meeting has put Pakistan at the center of the biggest story in the world, spotlighting its normally sleepy capital that has been preparing for days for high-profile delegations to arrive.
Ahead of the talks, many in Islamabad were still trying to get their heads around the fact that their country's diplomatic efforts actually worked.
"I'm a bit surprised," says 19-year-old Khizra Zaheer, standing in a parking lot of a shopping area near the center of the city. "When did Pakistan get so influential?"
That has been a central question in the past three weeks as Pakistan transitioned from a quiet go-between to an active participant in negotiations between the US and Iran, pulling in leaders from Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and China to support its peace efforts before putting forward a ceasefire plan. The true significance of Pakistan's intervention only became clear when both sides agreed to a pause shortly after a down-to-the-wire plea from the country's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif.
Police officers take position in Islamabad, Pakistan, to ensure security ahead of possible negotiations between Iran and the United States, Friday, April 10, 2026. Anjum Naveed/AP hide caption
President Trump and Iran's foreign ministry went on to name Sharif and Pakistani army chief Asim Munir, in their ceasefire announcements. "That was a very rare concurrence, because no other country enjoyed the same kind of trust from both parties," says Rasheed Wali Janjua, director of research at the Islamabad Policy Research Institute, a national security think-tank. "It's a fair assessment to say that both parties are looking for a way out."
The talks came as two U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyers passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, a U.S. official told NPR, marking the first transit of American warships since the start of the Iran war six weeks ago.
The official, who is not authorized to speak publicly, said this is the start of the process of reopening the Strait to commercial shipping.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said it had begun setting conditions to clear Iranian sea mines planted throughout the waterway.
"Today, we began the process of establishing a new passage and we will share this safe pathway with the maritime industry soon to encourage the free flow of commerce," said Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of CENTCOM.
Diaa Hadid contributed to this report from Mumbai. Rebecca Rosman contributed from London. Alana Wise contributed from Washington.
